<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    The growing demand for efficient CO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    conversion technologies in electrochemical systems has spurred the development of advanced catalysts and membrane designs. This study investigates the impact of hydrogen‐rich (H‐rich) skin layers, created through barbituric acid (BTA) modification, on the catalytic performance of Pt‐based and high‐entropy alloy (HEA) catalysts in anion exchange membrane (AEM) water electrolysis systems. The results show that BTA‐modified Pt and HEA catalysts significantly enhance CO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    conversion efficiency, achieving a maximum current density of 395 mA cm
                    <jats:sup>−2</jats:sup>
                    at 3 V and 40°C, alongside a CO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    removal rate of 39.3%. The H‐rich skin layer on the catalysts enhances surface hydrophilicity, increasing water molecule affinity and facilitating higher surface concentrations of H
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    O and CO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    , thereby accelerating crucial reaction steps in CO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    reduction. Furthermore, these skin layers enhance ionic transport via hydrogen‐bonding interactions, optimizing both the oxygen evolution reaction at the anode and CO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    reduction at the cathode. These findings suggest that the synergistic effects of H‐rich skin layers and HEA catalysts offer a promising strategy for improving the efficiency of electrochemical CO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    conversion processes, providing valuable insights into the design of high‐performance AEM systems.
                  </jats:p>
title: High‐Entropy Alloy Catalysts with Hydrogen‐Rich Skin Layers for Enhanced Carbon Dioxide Electroreduction in Anion Exchange Membrane Cells

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    The hydrogen spillover phenomenon provides an expeditious reaction pathway via hydrogen transfer from a strong H adsorption site to a weak H adsorption site, enabling a cost‐efficient hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) analogous to platinum with moderate H adsorption energy. Here, a high‐entropy oxychalcogenide (HEOC) comprising Co, Ni, Mo, W, O, Se, and Te is prepared by a two‐step electrochemical deposition for hydrogen spillover‐enhanced HER in acidic and alkaline water electrolysis. The anodic–cathodic reversal current enables the co‐deposition of cations and aliovalent anions, facilitating a glass structure with multiple active sites for hydrogen spillover. The HEOC exhibits low overpotentials of 52 and 57 mV to obtain a current density of 10 mA cm
                    <jats:sup>−2</jats:sup>
                    in acidic and alkaline media, respectively, and long‐term stability for 500 h. The electrochemical and analytical approaches elucidate the hydrogen transfer toward Mo/W−O sites in both acid and alkaline HERs. Meanwhile, the other sites act as hydrogen adsorption or water dissociation‐derived hydroxide adsorption sites, showing accommodable behavior in acidic and alkaline media. The HEOC exhibits a practically high current of 1 A cm
                    <jats:sup>−2</jats:sup>
                    at cell voltages of 1.78 and 1.89 V and long‐term stability for 100 h in proton and anion exchange membrane water electrolyzers, respectively.
                  </jats:p>
title: High‐Entropy Oxychalcogenide for Hydrogen Spillover Enhanced Hydrogen Evolution Reaction in Proton and Anion Exchange Membrane Water Electrolyzers

items.abstract: <jats:p>  	Anion exchange membrane water electrolyzers (AEMWEs) have gained significant attention due to their ability to operate with non-precious catalysts and construct compact, large cell stacks. Despite the superior hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) performance of Pt-based catalysts, their high cost and limited availability hinder widespread practical application. In this study, we develop a defect-rich, non-noble metal catalyst of NiMoFe/MoO₂ encapsulated in carbon shell (denoted as NiMoFe@C-e) as an HER electrocatalyst for AEMWEs. It is found that the structural disorder and surface carbon layer are effectively modulate the electronic structure to enhance HER performance. Electrochemical evaluation reveals outstanding HER activity, with ultralow overpotentials of 30 mV at 10 mA cm⁻², a small Tafel slope of 27 mV dec⁻¹, and exceptional stability for 2000 hours at 0.5 A cm⁻². A NiMoFe@C-e||FeNiCoMnCr layered double hydroxide (LDH) AEMWE cell achieves 0.5 A cm⁻² at 1.69 V in 1 M KOH at 60°C. The cell demonstrates remarkable durability, maintaining performance over 1000 hours with a degradation rate of only 0.19 mV h⁻¹. These findings highlight the potential of NiMoFe@C-e||FeNiCoMnCr LDH AEMWE for industrial applications and provide valuable insights for designing high-efficiency AEMWE systems.    </jats:p>
title: Defect-Rich NiMoFe/MoO₂ Encapsulated in Carbon Shell as High-Performance Hydrogen Evolution Reaction Electrocatalyst for Anion Exchange Membrane Water Electrolysis

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Alloys with multiple elements have emerged as advanced hydrogen/oxygen evolution reactions (HER/OER) electrocatalysts for anion exchange membrane water electrolysis (AEMWE) due to their excellent corrosion resistance, thermal stability, multiple active sites, and great inherent synergistic effect. However, the facile and rapid preparation of such alloys with high electrocatalytic activity remains challenging. Herein, a flash Joule‐heating strategy is conducted for ultrafast synthesis of RuVCoCuZnW medium‐entropy alloy with multiple elements (MEA) anchored on carbon nanotubes. The selective Zn volatilization during thermal shock generates abundant vacancies and mesoporous structures, creating a high‐density active surface. The optimized RuVCoCuZnW MEA exhibits exceptional bifunctional activity, requiring ultralow overpotentials of 231 mV (HER) and 435 mV (OER) to achieve ±500 mA cm
                    <jats:sup>−</jats:sup>
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                    in alkaline media, surpassing commercial Pt/C and RuO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    benchmarks. Furthermore, it demonstrates good stability in 1500 h long testing, with performance degradation exceeding the 2025 requirements of the US Department of Energy (≤40 µV h
                    <jats:sup>−1</jats:sup>
                    ). Through systematic characterization and density functional theory calculations, it is revealed that the Ru species and Zn vacancy sites synergistically optimize hydrogen and oxygen adsorption energy and accelerate reaction kinetics. This work provides a new approach for synthesizing nanoscale MEA electrocatalysts for clean energy conversion applications on a large‐scale basis for practical commercialization.
                  </jats:p>
title: Ultrafast Fabrication of Defect‐Rich Medium‐Entropy RuVCoCuZnW Alloy Nanoparticles for Industrial‐Current‐Density Anion Exchange Membrane Water Electrolysis

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Development of low‐cost, highly efficient and stable catalysts is critical for the prevalence of anion exchange membrane water electrolysis (AEMWE) technology for green hydrogen production. High entropy alloy (HEA)‐metal heterostructures (HEA‐Mo), taking advantage of the versatile active sites and multiple synergies between constituent elements of HEA and interfacial electronic interactions between HEA and metal, are promising bifunctional catalysts for high‐performance water electrolysis. Here, a FeCoNiCuMo HEA‐Mo heterostructured catalyst is synthesized, through supersaturation‐induced phase separation, for both anode and cathode of an AEMWE. The catalyst exhibits outstanding hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) (η
                    <jats:sub>10</jats:sub>
                    /η
                    <jats:sub>500</jats:sub>
                    of 24/140 mV) and oxygen evolution reaction (OER) (η
                    <jats:sub>10</jats:sub>
                    /η
                    <jats:sub>500</jats:sub>
                    of 175/325 mV) activities in 1 
                    <jats:sc>m</jats:sc>
                    KOH. The HEA‐Mo//HEA‐Mo based AEMWE delivers an ultrahigh current density of 2207 mA cm
                    <jats:sup>−2</jats:sup>
                    at 2.0 V and maintains stable operations at a commercially relevant high current density of 500 mA cm
                    <jats:sup>−2</jats:sup>
                    for 100 h with only 3.1% decay, demonstrating its excellent operation stability. HER activities are greatly enhanced through modulation of charge distributions with the decorated Mo, leading to better balanced hydrogen adsorption/desorption, together with the team up of Mo, a strong OH
                    <jats:sup>−</jats:sup>
                    adsorbent, for enhanced water dissociation to accelerate both the Volmer and Heyrovsky steps.
                  </jats:p>
title: Interface Engineering Effected Charge Redistribution within High Entropy Alloy‐Metal Heterostructured Catalyst Enables High Performance Anion Exchange Membrane Water Electrolysis

<jats:p> 	A decade of intensive research work on Anion Exchange Membrane Fuel Cells (AEMFCs) has finally yielded a high cell performance that is suitable for automotive applications. This achievement is mainly a result of the successful development of new anion-exchange membranes (AEMs) with high hydroxide conductivity (100 mS cm<jats:sup>-1</jats:sup> and above). Thanks to these high-performance membranes, AEMFCs with power densities higher than 1 W cm<jats:sup>-2</jats:sup> and limiting current densities above 4 A cm<jats:sup>-2</jats:sup> have been reached [1-2], which seemed far from possible only a couple of years ago. In spite of this remarkable progress on cell performance, it is the low performance stability during cell operation what hampers further development and implementation of AEMFCs. As it has been recently reviewed, most of the AEMFC performance stability data are still limited to <1000 h [3]. </jats:p>
               <jats:p>One of the key reasons in the reduction of cell performance is the presence of CO<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>. If pure oxygen is fed to the cathode, OH<jats:sup>–</jats:sup> alone is present and carries the charge. If ambient air is used instead of pure oxygen, carbonation processes occur in which OH<jats:sup>–</jats:sup> as a counteranion reacts with CO<jats:sub>2</jats:sub> present in air to produce (bi)carbonates. The main result of this carbonation process is a significant decrease in the effective anion conductivity in the AEM and, in turn, a reduction of the AEMFC power output [4-5]. While the carbonation process seems to be reversible [6-7], and so it could be mitigated, it may affect the chemical stability of the membrane, and in turn the cell performance stability. Furthermore, the hydroxide anions transported from the cathode to the anode may attack the positively charged functional groups of the polymeric membrane (and ionomer), neutralizing part of it and suppressing its anion-conducting capability. This process may actually cause irreversible performance losses during cell operation. To address this challenge, several new stable ionomeric materials have been proposed, and while they perform well in ex-situ chemical stability studies, their performance is still limited in real operating fuel cells. Although cation chemistry dictates the intrinsic chemical stability of the anion-conducting ionomeric materials, it was recently shown that the hydration level at which the fuel cell operates significantly affects the chemical degradation [8-9]. This relationship between local cell hydration and ionomeric material degradation has been analyzed in modelling studies, providing further insights about the critical role of water on the performance stability [10]. </jats:p>
               <jats:p>This talk will discuss the relationship between water, CO<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>, membrane/ionomer degradation, and their impact on the AEMFC performance stability. A unique recently developed model capable of predicting the performance stability of AEMFCs will be also presented. By using membranes with achievable targeted properties, the model predicts an AEMFC life-time higher than 8000 h [10], suitable for automotive applications. </jats:p>

               <jats:p>[2] L. Q. Wang, E. Magliocca, E. L. Cunningham, W. E. Mustain, S. D. Poynton, R. Escudero-Cid, M. M. Nasef, J. Ponce-Gonzalez, R. Bance-Souahli, R. C. T. Slade, D. K. Whelligan, and J. R. Varcoe; Green Chem. 19, 831-843, 2017. </jats:p>
               <jats:p>[3] D. R. Dekel; J. Power Sources 375, 158-169, 2018. </jats:p>
               <jats:p>[4] N. Ziv, W. E. Mustain, and D. R. Dekel; ChemSusChem 11(7), 1136-1150, 2018. </jats:p>
               <jats:p>[5] U. Krewer, C. Weinzierl, N. Ziv, and D. R. Dekel; Electrochimica Acta 263, 433-446, 2018. </jats:p>
               <jats:p>[6] N. Ziv and D. R. Dekel; Electrochemistry Communications 88, 109-113, 2018 </jats:p>
               <jats:p>[7] S. Gottesfeld, D. R. Dekel, M. Page, C. Bae, Y. Yan, P. Zelenay, and Y.-S. Kim; J. Power Sources 375, 170-184, 2018. </jats:p>
               <jats:p>[8] C. E. Diesendruck and D. R. Dekel, Current Opinion in Electrochem. 9, 173–178, 2018. </jats:p>
